title: Modak
hookLine: why he's always eating; the sweet as a gift that returns
carry: prasad: the offering comes back as grace
tomorrow: who would try to eat the sun for breakfast?
last: GANESHA RIDES DESIRE; IT DOESN'T RIDE HIM.

lines: A LITTLE BOX FOR THE ROAD.
A DUMPLING LIKE A FLOWER BUD.
A FEAST THAT CAN'T FILL HIM.
cards: Leave a wedding or a festival and sometimes someone presses a little box into your hands: something sweet for the road. Ganesha has his own, and he never seems to put it down.
In many images there's a sweet in his hand, a modak: a little dumpling of rice flour, pinched shut at the top like a flower bud, filled with coconut and jaggery.
One of his names means the one who loves modaks, and at his festival, Ganesh Chaturthi, families make them by the trayful. People tell a story about that appetite.
Kubera, a rich god proud of his wealth, throws Ganesha a feast to show off. Ganesha eats every dish, every pot, and he's still hungry.

teach.b: What finally fills him is tiny: a handful of plain food, given with love. The story isn't in one fixed text; it's the kind families pass down.
But it points at the word prasad: grace, a gift given freely.
At a temple or a home shrine, food is offered to the god, sits before the image a while, then comes back and is shared with everyone there. Not leftovers. The same food, returned as a blessing.

People often take it with the right hand, or with both hands cupped. And a detail worth repeating: in older Sanskrit, prasada also means clarity, a calm and settled mind. The gift and the grace are one word.
Now hold the week up to the light. A god welcomed into clay. A mother's grief that stopped the universe.
A new face, honored first. A slow circle around his parents. A broken tusk for sacred words.

teach.h: PRASAD: THE OFFERING COMES BACK AS GRACE.
teach.b: And a sweet, handed back as grace. Seven days with one god.

how: At temples and home shrines Hindus offer food to the deity and then share it as prasad; at Ganesh Chaturthi many families make modaks, offer them to Ganesha, and give them out to family and neighbors.

o: food offered to God, then shared back as a blessing
a vow made to a god in return for a granted wish
a fast kept before a festival to earn a blessing

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: the rich god whose feast fell short
offered food handed back as grace
his festival, modaks by the tray

s: prasad is just the leftovers from the offering
the same food, returned as a blessing, and shared.
in the story, Kubera's feast satisfies Ganesha
nothing Kubera owns can fill him; a small handful given with love does.

the gift and the grace are the same word.

games.q: you bring sweets to a friend's family dinner. her grandmother sets them at the home shrine, then hands half back to you. what's happening?
o: she's politely returning them; there's more than enough.
your gift has come back as prasad, a blessing to share.
she's checking whether you'll be polite and refuse.
games.why: offered, then handed back: that's prasad. the offering comes back, and you share it.

practice: If there's anything to eat near you, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a square of chocolate, hold it and smell it before anything else. Break it in two, and set half aside for someone before you taste yours.
Eat your half slowly, and notice what it's like to taste something you've already given away. Some people first offer a meal to God; others offer it to the person across the table.

wordCard.voice: Prasad: grace. Food offered, then handed back as a blessing, made to be shared. The last word of the week.

orig.note: Sanskrit: grace, favor, clearness; the food handed back after an offering.

carryVoice: Last line of Ganesha's week: prasad, the offering comes back as grace. Seven days, seven stories, one god.

sources.ref: popular Ganesha tradition (Kubera's feast; Ganesha as lover of modaks)
